Not sure I agree with this sentiment. The place to find truths is nonfiction. Fiction, even those works considered great, tend to be pretty poor at helping you model the world accurately.

The story of Romeo and Juliette tells more than one Great Truth. Obviously it's not a truth about two literal houses, or even about the political situation of its day. The truths it tells are these:

  • Pride can lead one to destroy precious things.

  • Conflict is often justified only from within a group that's involved. Stepping one's point of view outside of a conflict can reveal the forest one has been missing for the trees.

  • Death is permanent, and suicide can result in unrecoverable mistakes.

Nonfiction (in this case it would be philosophy) may proclaim these to be true, but only good fiction can allow a person to internalize such lessons, the difference between understanding chemistry and smelling a rose.

Now using the angular resolution equation, (theta) = (lamda) / D... theta = 1.67*10^ -5, lamda = 500nm, D is unknown

= .037 m
